stories.title: Law Firm Greenberg Traurig Takes 25K SF at Related Ross Dev in West Palm
stories.excerpt: Law firm Greenberg Traurig is relocating to another Related Ross building in Downtown West Palm Beach, Fla. The firm signed a 10-year lease to occupy about 25,000 square feet at the 15 CityPlace office development, which remains under construction, the tenant announced. The deal spans the entire 12th floor of the 25-story project. Move-in is scheduled for fall 2027. “The move reflects our long-term commitment to the West Palm Beach market and positions us to meet increasing client demand throughout Palm Beach County and beyond,” Tracy Gerber, co-managing shareholder of Greenberg Traurig’s West Palm Beach office, said in a statement. 15 CityPlace, and the neighboring 10 CityPlace, are expected to be completed next year after developer Related Ross secured a $772 million construction debt package last year. Health care provider Cleveland Clinic has already pre-leased 125,000 square feet at 15 CityPlace, which will span about 500,000 square feet. The law firm is currently stationed at Philips Point, where it leases roughly 30,000 square feet. Related Ross, led by Stephen Ross, purchased the 448,914-square-foot office for $282 million in 2021. The two-building complex, which dates back to 1985, is currently undergoing a $120 million renovation. Even as Greenberg Traurig departs, the building has nabbed new tenants: global index provider MSCI taking 7,500 square feet, investment bank Solomon Partners taking 4,200 square feet, and Integrity Pro Consulting taking 1,300 square feet. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Greenberg Traurig signs 10-year, 25K SF lease at Related Ross' 15 CityPlace, West Palm Beach.
Cleveland Clinic pre-leased 125K SF at same 500K SF project; $772M construction debt secured.
Law firm move signals confidence in Downtown West Palm Beach office market through 2027.
stories.summary: Greenberg Traurig is relocating within West Palm Beach to a Related Ross office tower under construction, signing a 10-year lease for the entire 12th floor (25,000 SF) at 15 CityPlace, with move-in in fall 2027. The 500K SF, 25-story project is anchored by Cleveland Clinic's 125K SF pre-lease and backed by $772M in construction financing. The law firm's long-term commitment reflects expanding client demand across Palm Beach County.
stories.impact: Strong office anchoring and professional services expansion in West Palm Beach's downtown core signals sustained employment and population in-migration to the market. This demand validation de-risks multifamily development in proximate submarkets; developers should monitor absorption trends and job growth in law, healthcare, and corporate sectors to time residential product delivery and pricing in West Palm Beach and broader South Florida.

stories.title: Law Firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee Leases 11K SF at 7 World Trade Center
stories.excerpt: Washington D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee is establishing a new office in New York City. The firm, which specializes in high stakes trials, investigations and crisis management, has inked an 11,167-square-foot lease on the 34th floor of 7 World Trade Center, developer and landlord Silverstein Properties announced Monday. Silverstein did not disclose the length of the lease or the asking rent. However, a source close to the deal noted asking rents in the building range from $100 to $150 per square foot. “We are excited to welcome our teams and our clients into our new Manhattan office later this year,” Jeannie Rhee, managing partner of Dunn Isaacson Rhee, said in a statement. “7 World Trade Center offers the ideal combination of thoughtful design, functionality, and a premier location in the heart of the Financial District and a stone’s throw to the Southern District of New York courthouse.” Dunn Isaacson Rhee will relocate from 11 Park Place, also in the Financial District. It’s unclear when the firm will make the move. Dunn Isaacson Rhee did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Lisa Ann Pollakowski, Cory Gahr and Richard Plehn from Lee & Associates represented the tenant in the deal, while Silverstein was represented in-house by Keith A. Cody, Gordon Hough and Harlan Strader, as well as by CBRE’s MaryAnn Tighe. Lee & Associates did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. “Dunn Isaacson Rhee represents the caliber of organization that continues to define 7 World Trade Center as one of Downtown Manhattan’s premier office destinations,” Silverstein’s Cody said in a statement. “Today’s leading firms are seeking workplaces that reflect their brand, support their people and provide an exceptional experience for their clients. bullets: DC-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee opens NYC office with 11.2K SF lease at 7 World Trade.
Asking rents at Silverstein property range $100–$150/SF; firm relocates from 11 Park Place.
Firm specializes in high-stakes litigation and crisis management; new office targets Southern District courthouse proximity.
stories.summary: Dunn Isaacson Rhee, a Washington D.C.-based litigation and crisis management firm, is establishing its first Manhattan office with an 11,167 SF lease on the 34th floor of 7 World Trade Center. Asking rents at the Silverstein Properties-owned tower range from $100 to $150 per square foot. The firm is relocating from 11 Park Place in the Financial District and will occupy space later in 2025.
stories.impact: Out-of-state professional services firms establishing NYC footholds signal continued labor demand and talent migration to Manhattan's Financial District. This office expansion does not directly drive residential demand but indicates workforce stability in the metro; developers should monitor whether such professional services clustering sustains rental demand in downtown-proximate multifamily assets and residential neighborhoods serving Financial District workers.

stories.title: Alliance for Downtown New York Inks 14K SF at 42 Broadway
stories.excerpt: Nonprofit group Alliance For Downtown New York has expanded its Lower Manhattan footprint to 42 Broadway. The Downtown Alliance, which manages the area’s business improvement district, secured a 14,420-square-foot lease at the Financial District tower, according to a recent CBRE office market report. The Downtown Alliance plans to relocate its operations division to the 22-story office building, a spokesperson for the nonprofit told CO. The nonprofit’s corporate headquarters remain housed roughly three blocks north at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. JLL’s John Wheeler and his team at JLL represented the tenant in the negotiations. A spokesperson for the team did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The lease terms were not disclosed, but office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91 per square foot in July, according to the CBRE report. A spokesperson for the landlord, Avi Schron‘s Cammeby’s International Group, confirmed the recent transaction to CO, adding that the space is still under construction. It was not immediately clear whether Cammeby’s International Group worked with any outside brokers. Cammeby’s 42 Broadway is located near the intersection of Broadway and Morris Street. Appellate service organization Office of the Appellate Defender relocated there in November, joining a tenant roster that includes office suite provider TKO Suites, chiropractor Prestige Health and Wellness, dental practice DDS Group and cafe Gregorys Coffee. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Alliance for Downtown New York (BID) leases 14.4K SF at 42 Broadway, Lower Manhattan.
Operations division relocates; HQ remains at Silverstein's 120 Broadway three blocks north.
Lower Manhattan office asking rents average $61.91/SF as of July; lease terms undisclosed.
stories.summary: The Alliance for Downtown New York, the Financial District's business improvement district, has leased 14,420 SF at 42 Broadway to relocate its operations division, while maintaining its corporate headquarters at 120 Broadway. The move expands the nonprofit's Lower Manhattan footprint across two Silverstein Properties locations. Lower Manhattan office asking rents averaged $61.91 per square foot as of July.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; the BID's investment in Lower Manhattan real estate reinforces institutional commitment to the Financial District's long-term viability and revitalization. However, sustained BID operations and amenity management are indirect supports for residential demand in adjacent neighborhoods; developers should monitor whether such anchor tenant stability justifies new or repositioned multifamily product in downtown Brooklyn and Hudson Yards-adjacent markets.

stories.title: New York’s Rent Freeze Was Only An Aftershock. This 2019 Law Was The Quake.
stories.excerpt: Jose Tur owns two rent-stabilized rental buildings in Manhattan’s Washington Heights with a total of 45 units. The properties have been in his family for over 30 years, and the mortgages are fully paid off. But Tur tells Commercial Observer that despite this, while he’s reluctant to give an exact number, “more than two or three” units have been sitting empty for an average of over two years. That’s because, according to Tur’s estimates, it would cost anywhere from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit to return them to a livable state, and that’s money he can’t justify spending in return for the stabilized rent amounts in today’s environment. “Some of them require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Tur, who has testified about these financial challenges to New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). “[Oftentimes] the plumbing’s really old because a tenant has lived there for 10 to 15 years, and you have to do the electrical and then lead abatement, which really increases the tally on the job.” Tur says that the $30,000 estimate is before taking into account more cosmetic fixes like cabinets, tiles and so forth, meaning the total is often closer to $60,000 for a one-bedroom apartment. Given all this, the fate of his currently empty apartments is uncertain. With no financial relief in sight, it is likely the units will not be lived in again for the foreseeable future, removed from the rolls of New York’s livable spaces — and from Tur’s income-producing properties — as if they had never existed. The RGB approved a freeze on rent increases for one- and two-year leases for the city’s rent-stabilized apartments in June for lease terms beginning on Oct. 1 or later. bullets: NYC rent-stabilized landlord holds 2–3+ vacant units for 2+ years due to $30K–$60K rehab costs.
Stabilized rents cannot justify capital spend; 2019 Housing Stability law (RGB authority over increases) is root cause.
Owner reluctant to commit to stabilized stock; units remain dark despite paid-off mortgages and market demand.
stories.summary: A Manhattan rent-stabilized landlord with 45 units in Washington Heights has left more than two or three units vacant for over two years because the $30,000 to $60,000 per-unit rehabilitation costs (plumbing, electrical, lead abatement) cannot be economically justified against capped stabilized rents. The owner attributes the financial trap to the 2019 Housing Stability law, which gave the Rent Guidelines Board authority to set annual increases; despite owning the properties outright with no mortgage, the landlord cannot justify reinvestment.
stories.impact: Rent stabilization regulations are creating a perverse outcome: reduction in effective supply as owners mothball units rather than reinvest, shrinking the stabilized stock available to lower-income tenants. This artificially constrains overall housing supply in Manhattan and may drive marginal renters upmarket into market-rate buildings, supporting prices in new and unregulated multifamily product. Developers should model future policy risk in NYC underwriting; if stabilization expands to market-rate stock or rent control tightens further, returns on new supply will compress and development velocity will slow.

stories.title: Local Developer Plans to Build a School at 1000 University Avenue in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: School is in session in the Bronx, or at least it will be. Kiumarz Geula, principal of real estate development firm Pillar Property Management, has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to build a seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The plans were filed with the DOB on Aug. 5. Geula did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Jonathan Imani of IMC Architecture, the registered architect on the project, also did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. The DOB plans have few details about the scope of the work coming to the vacant Bronx property. The plans call for the construction of a 64,366-square-foot, 108-foot tall building with a cafeteria and recreation space. No other details are available. Pillar Property Management isn’t the only developer planning to bring a new school building to the Bronx. In June, Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures secured a $60 million debt package to acquire and build a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Ripco Real Estate’s James Murad, who arranged the financing for that deal, told CO at the time that the project reflects “the growing demand for high-quality educational facilities in underserved communities and the continued appeal of mission-driven real estate investments.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pillar Property Management files plans for 7-story, 64.4K SF school building in Highbridge, Bronx.
Project at 1000 University Avenue; filed Aug. 5; no additional project details disclosed.
Apex Development and Knickpoint Ventures separately secured $60M debt for charter school at 1780 East Tremont.
stories.summary: Pillar Property Management has filed construction plans with NYC's Department of Buildings for a seven-story, 64,366 SF school building (108 feet tall) at 1000 University Avenue in Highbridge, the Bronx. The project includes cafeteria and recreation space but no other details are available. A separate developer team (Apex/Knickpoint) recently closed $60M debt for a charter school at 1780 East Tremont in the same borough.
stories.impact: Charter school and educational facility development in the Bronx signals confidence in population stability and youth demographic growth in the borough. New school buildings anchor neighborhood revitalization and attract families, indirectly supporting multifamily demand in Highbridge and surrounding Bronx submarkets. Developers should track school openings and enrollment trends as leading indicators of residential in-migration; submarkets with recent school investment and institutional anchoring may justify new family-oriented or affordable multifamily product.
